title: FUNCTORIALITY OF THE CATEGORIES OF SHEAVES

pages.title: FUNCTORIALITY OF THE CATEGORIES OF SHEAVES

blocks.html:
Exposé III
FUNCTORIALITY OF THE CATEGORIES OF SHEAVESby J.L. Verdier

In I 5, we studied the behaviour of the categories of presheaves with respect to functors between the categories of arguments. In this exposé, we extend this study to the case of sites and categories of sheaves (no. 1 and 2). After introducing the induced topology (no. 3), we take up in no. 4 the comparison lemma, which will play an important role in Exp. IV. In no. 5, we study, for the patient reader, certain commutative diagrams connected with the localized categories (of type \(C/X\)). In Theorem 5.1 we make smallness hypotheses on the categories under consideration. These hypotheses are not, in general, satisfied by the sites encountered in practice (\(\mathcal{U}\)-sites). This forces upon us a few contortions (4.2, 4.3, 4.4).
1. Continuous functors

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. We say that \(u\) is continuous if for every sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(C'\), the presheaf \(X \mapsto F \circ u(X)\) on \(C\) is a sheaf.
This notion of continuity depends a priori on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) for which the two sites are \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites. Proposition 1.5 shows that it does not depend on it.

We denote by \(i : \widetilde{C} \to \widehat{C}\) (resp. \(i' : \widetilde{C}' \to \widehat{C}'\)) the canonical inclusion functor of sheaves into presheaves. By Definition 1.1, the functor \(u\) is continuous if and only if there exists a functor \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) such that the equality \(i u_s = u^* i'\) holds (with \(u^* F = F \circ u\) (I 5.0)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2

Let \(C\) be a small site, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The functor \(u\) is continuous.

  2. ii)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) covering \(X\), the morphism \(u_! R \to u(X)\) is bicovering in \(\widehat{C}'\) (II 5.2 and I 5.1).(∗)

  3. iii)

    For every bicovering family \(H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), of \(\widehat{C}\), the family of the \(u_! H_i \to u_! K\), \(i \in I\), is bicovering in \(\widehat{C}'\).

  4. iv)

    There exists a functor \(u^s : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\), commuting with inductive limits and "extending \(u\)", i.e. such that the diagram of canonical functors \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_C} & C' \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_{C'}} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' } \] is commutative up to isomorphism.

Moreover, when \(C\) is no longer necessarily a small site, but a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, we always have i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) iv) and the functor \(u^s\) of iv) is necessarily a left adjoint of the functor \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\), and is consequently determined up to unique isomorphism.
Proof: The proof of i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) iv) when \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site will be given in 4.2. Suppose \(C\) small. It is clear that iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii).

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) iii): Let \(H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), be a bicovering family of \(\widehat{C}\). For every sheaf \(F\) on \(C'\), the presheaf \(u^* F\) (I 5.0) is a sheaf on \(C\). Hence (II 5.3) the canonical map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(K, u^* F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(H_i, u^* F) , \] is bijective. By adjunction (I 5.1), we deduce that the canonical map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(u_! K, F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(u_! H_i, F) \] is bijective. Consequently (II 5.3) the family \(u_! H_i \to u_! K\), \(i \in I\), is bicovering.

ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i): Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\), \(R \hookrightarrow X\) a covering sieve, \(F\) a sheaf on \(C'\). By (II 5.3), the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(u_! X, F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(u_! R, F) \] is bijective. By adjunction (I 5.1), we deduce that the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X, u^* F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(R, u^* F) \] is bijective. Consequently \(u^* F\) is a sheaf.

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) iv): We use the usual notation \(a\) and \(i\) (resp. \(a'\) and \(i'\)) for the functors "associated sheaf" and "inclusion into presheaves". For every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\), we set \(u^s G = a' u_! i G\). For every sheaf \(F\) on \(C'\), we have the following sequence of natural isomorphisms: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(G, u_s F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(iG, i u_s F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(iG, u^* i'F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(u_! iG, i'F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(a' u_! iG, F) . \] (The first isomorphism comes from the fact that \(i\) is fully faithful; the second isomorphism comes from the definition of \(u_s\); the third and fourth isomorphisms are obtained by adjunction). Consequently \(u^s\) is left adjoint to \(u_s\). In particular \(u^s\) commutes with inductive limits. For every presheaf \(K\) on \(C\) and every sheaf \(F\) on \(C'\), we have the following sequence of natural isomorphisms: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(u^s a K, F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(a K, u_s F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(K, i u_s F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(K, u^* i'F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(u_! K, i'F) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(a' u_! K, F) \] (the third isomorphism comes from the definition of \(u_s\); the others are obtained by adjunction); whence a functorial isomorphism \(u^s a K \simeq a' u_! K\). In particular, using this isomorphism when \(K\) is representable, we obtain, taking I 5.4 3) into account, a diagram commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_C} & C' \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_{C'}} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' } \]

iv) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii): Let \(h : C \to \widehat{C}\) (resp. \(h' : C' \to \widehat{C}'\)) be the functor which associates to an object the presheaf it represents. Consider the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{h} & C' \ar[d]^-{h'} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[r]^-{u_!} \ar[d]_-{a} & \widehat{C}' \ar[d]^-{a'} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' . } \]

The upper square is commutative (I 5.4 3)) and we have \(a h = \varepsilon_C\), \(a' h' = \varepsilon_{C'}\). For every object \(K\) of \(\widehat{C}\), we have a canonical isomorphism (I 3.4): \[ \varinjlim_{(h(X) \to K)\, \in\, \mathrm{ob}(C/K)} h(X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } K . \] Since the functors \(u_!\), \(u^s\), \(a\) and \(a'\) commute with inductive limits, we deduce isomorphisms: \[ \varinjlim_{(h(X) \to K)\, \in\, \mathrm{ob}(C/K)} u^s a h(X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u^s a K , \] \[ \varinjlim_{(h(X) \to K)\, \in\, \mathrm{ob}(C/K)} a' u_! h(X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } a' u_! K . \] We have \(u_! h = h' u\) and, by hypothesis, we have an isomorphism \(a' h' u \simeq u^s a h\), whence an isomorphism: \[ u^s a K \simeq a' u_! K , \] which one immediately checks is functorial in \(K\). The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C} \ar[r]^-{u_!} \ar[d]_-{a} & \widehat{C}' \ar[d]^-{a'} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' , } \] is therefore commutative up to isomorphism. Since \(a i\) is isomorphic to the identity functor, we have an isomorphism \(u^s \simeq a' u_! i\), whence the uniqueness of \(u^s\). Let \(v : H \to K\) be a bicovering morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). Then \(a(v)\) is an isomorphism (II 5.3) and consequently \(a' u_!(v)\) (isomorphic to \(u^s a(v)\)) is an isomorphism. Hence \(u_!(v)\) is transformed by \(a'\) into an isomorphism, and consequently \(u_!(v)\) is bicovering (II 5.3), whence ii).
The additional assertion, in the case \(C\) small, has been proved in the course of the proof, q.e.d.

The functor \(u^s : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\) of 1.2 iv) can often be interpreted as an "inverse image" functor for a "morphism of topoi" \(\widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\), cf. IV 4.9. Its properties are summarized in the following proposition:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3

Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a continuous functor between a small site \(C\) and a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site \(C'\).

  1. 1)

    The functor \(u^s\) is left adjoint to the functor \(u_s\).

  2. 2)

    We have a canonical isomorphism \(u^s \simeq a' u_! i\).

  3. 3)

    We have a canonical isomorphism \(u^s a \simeq a' u_!\).

  4. 4)

    The functor \(u^s\) commutes with inductive limits.

  5. 5)

    When the functor \(u_!\) is left exact (cf. I 5.4 4)), so is the functor \(u^s\). More generally the functor \(u^s\) commutes with the types of finite projective limits with which the functor \(u_!\) commutes.

Proof: Assertions 1), 2), 3), 4) have been proved in the course of the proof of 1.2. Assertion 5) follows from isomorphism 2), taking into account that \(i\) commutes with projective limits and that \(a'\) commutes with finite projective limits (II 4.1).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.4

By combining I 5.4 3) and 1.3 3) we obtain a diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{h} & C' \ar[d]^-{h'} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[r]^-{u_!} \ar[d]_-{a} & \widehat{C}' \ar[d]^-{a'} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' , } \] where the upper square is commutative and the lower square commutative up to isomorphism. But the functors \(a\), \(a'\), \(u_!\), \(u^s\) are only defined up to isomorphism. The reader may verify that one can choose the functors \(a\), \(a'\) and \(u^s\) in such a way that:

  1. 1)

    The composite functors \(a h\) and \(a' h'\) are injective on the sets of objects;

  2. 2)

    the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{a h} & C' \ar[d]^-{a' h'} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' } \] is commutative.

More precisely, one can choose the functors \(a\) and \(a'\) so as to satisfy condition 1). The functors \(a\) and \(a'\) being chosen, one can choose the functor \(u^s\) so as to satisfy condition 2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.5

Let \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\) be two universes, \(C\) and \(C'\) two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites, \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. Then \(u\) is continuous relative to \(\mathcal{U}\) if and only if it is continuous relative to \(\mathcal{V}\). Moreover, when \(u\) is continuous, we denote by \(u^s_{\mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(u^s_{\mathcal{V}}\)) the functor between categories of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves) introduced in 1.2 iv). Then the diagram \[ (1.5.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[r]^-{u^s_{\mathcal{U}}} \ar[d] & \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[d] \\ \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \ar[r]_-{u^s_{\mathcal{V}}} & \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{V}} , } \] where the vertical functors are the canonical inclusion functors, is commutative up to canonical isomorphism.

Proof. We shall give the proof only in the case where \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. The general case will be proved in 4.3. It is clear that if the functor \(u^*\) transforms every \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaf on \(C'\) into a \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaf on \(C\), it transforms every \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf on \(C'\) into a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf on \(C\). Suppose that \(u^*\) transforms every \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf on \(C'\) into a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf on \(C\). We denote by \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \hookrightarrow \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) (resp. \(\widehat{C}'_{\mathcal{U}} \hookrightarrow \widehat{C}'_{\mathcal{V}}\)) the categories of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves and \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves, by \(u_{\mathcal{U}!}\) and \(u_{\mathcal{V}!}\) the "inverse image" functors for \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves and \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves respectively. We have a commutative diagram (cf. the explicit construction of \(u_!\) in I 5.1): \[ (*) \qquad \xymatrix{ \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[r]^-{u_{\mathcal{U}!}} \ar[d] & \widehat{C}'_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[d] \\ \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \ar[r]_-{u_{\mathcal{V}!}} & \widehat{C}'_{\mathcal{V}} . } \] The inclusion functors of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves into \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves are fully faithful and commute with projective limits. It then follows from (II 5.1 i)) that a bicovering morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves is a bicovering morphism of \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves. Let then \(R \hookrightarrow X\) be a sieve covering an object \(X\) of \(C\). By 1.2 ii), the morphism \(u_{\mathcal{U}!} R \to u_{\mathcal{U}!} X\) is bicovering. Using the commutativity of (*) and what precedes, we deduce that the morphism \(u_{\mathcal{V}!} R \to u_{\mathcal{V}!} X\) is bicovering. Consequently (1.2), the functor \(u^*\) transforms the \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves on \(C'\) into \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves on \(C\). The commutativity of 1.5.1 then follows from the commutativity of (*), from II 3.6 and from 1.3 2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.6

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites, \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. Consider the conditions:

  1. i)

    \(u\) is continuous (cf. 1.1 and 1.2).

  2. ii)

    For every covering family \((X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), of \(C\), the family \((u X_i \to u X)\), \(i \in I\), of \(C'\), is covering.

We have the implication i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii).

Suppose that the topology of \(C\) can be defined by a pretopology \(T\) (II 1.3) and that the functor \(u\) commutes with fibre products.(∗) Then conditions i) and ii) are equivalent and are equivalent to the following condition:

  1. iii)

    The functor \(u\) transforms the covering families of \(T\) into covering families of \(C'\).

In particular, suppose that in \(C\) the fibre products are representable and that the functor \(u\) commutes with fibre products. Then conditions i) and ii) are equivalent.

Proof. Let us show that i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). Let \(X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), be a covering family of \(C\). For every sheaf \(F\) on \(C'\), \(u^* F\) is a sheaf. Consequently, the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X, u^* F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i, u^* F) \] is injective (II 5.1). Whence an injective map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(u_! X, F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(u_! X_i, F) . \] Hence the family \(u_! X_i \to u_! X\), \(i \in I\), is covering in \(C'\) (II 5.1).

Every covering family of the pretopology \(T\) is a covering family of \(C\), whence ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) iii). Let us show that iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and \(X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), a covering family of \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) (II 1.3). The morphisms \(X_i \to X\) are squarable and the functor \(u\) commutes with fibre products. Consequently, the fibre products \(u(X_i) \times_{u(X)} u(X_j)\) are representable and canonically isomorphic to \(u(X_i \times_X X_j)\). Let \(F\) be a sheaf on \(C'\). Then the diagram of sets: \[ F(u(X)) \longrightarrow \prod_i F(u(X_i)) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} F(u(X_i \times_X X_j)) \] is exact (II 2.1, I 3.5 and I 2.12). Consequently the diagram of sets \[ u^* F(X) \longrightarrow \prod_i u^* F(X_i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} u^* F(X_i \times_X X_j) \] is exact. Hence \(u^* F\) is a sheaf (II 2.4), whence i). The last assertion of 1.6 follows from what precedes and from the fact that, when the fibre products are representable in \(C\), all the covering families of \(C\)(1) define on \(C\) a pretopology whose associated topology is the topology of \(C\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.7

Let \(C\) be a small site, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(u : C \to C'\) a continuous functor. Let \(\gamma\) be an algebraic structure defined by finite projective limits, such that in the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive limits are representable.(2) We use the notation of proposition II 6.4. The functor \(u_s\) commutes with projective limits and consequently defines a functor \(u_s^\gamma : \widetilde{C}'_\gamma \to \widetilde{C}_\gamma\). The functor \(u_s^\gamma\) admits a left adjoint \(u^s_\gamma\) which possesses the following properties:

  1. 1)

    We have a canonical isomorphism \(u^s_\gamma \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } a'_\gamma u_{\gamma !} i_\gamma\), and \(u^s_\gamma\) commutes with the finite projective limits with which \(u_{\gamma !}\) commutes.

  2. 2)

    We have a canonical isomorphism \(u^s_\gamma a_\gamma \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } a'_\gamma u_{\gamma !}\).

  3. 3)

    The functor \(u^s_\gamma\) commutes with inductive limits.

  4. 4)

    If \(u^s\) is left exact, the diagram (notation of II 6.3.0) \[ \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C}_\gamma \ar[r]^-{u^s_\gamma} \ar[d]_-{\mathrm{esj}^\sim} & \widetilde{C}'_\gamma \ar[d]^-{\mathrm{esj}'^\sim} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' } \] is commutative up to isomorphism and the functor \(u^s_\gamma\) is exact.

  5. 5)

    Suppose that the functor \(\mathrm{esj}^\sim\) (resp. \(\mathrm{esj}'^\sim\)) possesses a left adjoint \(\mathrm{Lib}^\sim\) (resp. \(\mathrm{Lib}'^\sim\)) (II 6.5). We have a canonical isomorphism: \[ u^s_\gamma \mathrm{Lib}^\sim \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Lib}'^\sim u^s . \]

Moreover, when \(C\) is not necessarily a small site but a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, the functor \(u_s^\gamma\) admits a left adjoint \(u^s_\gamma\). Finally, if \(\mathcal{V}\) is a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\) and if \(u^s_{\gamma, \mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(u^s_{\gamma, \mathcal{V}}\)) denotes the left adjoint of \(u_s\) relative to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)), the following diagram, analogous to diagram 1.5.1: \[ (1.7.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C}_{\gamma, \mathcal{U}} \ar[r]^-{u^s_{\gamma, \mathcal{U}}} \ar[d] & \widetilde{C}'_{\gamma, \mathcal{U}} \ar[d] \\ \widetilde{C}_{\gamma, \mathcal{V}} \ar[r]_-{u^s_{\gamma, \mathcal{V}}} & \widetilde{C}'_{\gamma, \mathcal{V}} } \] is commutative up to canonical isomorphism.
Proof. The proof, in the case where \(C\) is a small site, is left to the reader. It will be completed in 4.3 in the case where \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.html:
Notation 1.8

From now on we shall use the notation \(u_s\) to denote the functor \(u_s^\gamma\). This notation cannot give rise to confusion, since the functor \(u_s\) (defined on sheaves of sets) commutes with finite projective limits.

Similarly, when \(u^s\) is left exact, we shall use the notation \(u^s\) to denote the functor \(u^s_\gamma\). This abuse of notation is justified by 1.7 4).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 1.9.1

Let \(X\) be a small topological space. We denote by \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) the category of open sets of \(X\) (the objects of \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) are the open subsets of \(X\), the morphisms of \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) are the inclusions) equipped with the canonical topology. A family \((U_i \subset U)\), \(i \in I\), is covering if and only if the open sets \(U_i\) cover \(U\) (II 2.6). The sheaves of sets on \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) are therefore the sheaves of sets in the sense of [TF]. Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a continuous map. We deduce from it a functor \(f^{-1} : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y) \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)\): for every open set \(U\) of \(Y\), \(f^{-1}(U)\) is the inverse image of \(U\) under the map \(f\). The functor \(f^{-1}\) is a continuous functor (1.6). The functor \(f^{-1}_s : \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim}\) is the direct image functor for sheaves, in the sense of [TF]. The functor \((f^{-1})^s : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim}\) is the inverse image functor for sheaves in the sense of [TF]. The functor \((f^{-1})^s\) commutes with finite projective limits, thanks to 1.3 5).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 1.9.2

Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(Y \hookrightarrow X\) an open set of \(X\). Every open set of \(Y\) is an open set of \(X\), whence a functor \(\varphi : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y) \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)\). The functor \(\varphi\) is continuous (1.6). The functor \(\varphi_s : \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim}\) is the "restriction to \(Y\)" functor. The functor \(\varphi^s_{\mathrm{ab}} : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim}\) (II 6.3.3, I 1.7) is the "extension by zero outside \(Y\)" functor introduced in [TF]. The functor \(\varphi^s : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim}\) (1.3) is analogous to the "extension by zero" functor; for every sheaf \(H\) on \(Y\) and every point \(y \in Y\), the stalk at \(y\) of \(\varphi^s H\) is canonically isomorphic to the stalk at \(y\) of \(H\); for every point \(x \in X\), \(x \notin Y\), the stalk at \(x\) of \(\varphi^s H\) is empty. The functor \(\varphi^s\) is called the "extension by the empty set outside \(Y\)" functor. The functor \(\varphi^s\) commutes with fibre products and with finite products over a non-empty index set, but it does not transform the final object of \(\mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim}\) into the final object of \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim}\).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 1.9.3

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two small sites, \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories which transforms every covering family of \(C\) into a covering family of \(C'\). The functor \(u\) is not continuous in general (cf. however 1.6). Here is a counterexample. Let \(S\) be a set of infinite cardinality in the universe \(\mathcal{U}\), and \(C\) the full subcategory of the category of sets whose objects are the finite, non-empty subsets of \(S\). We equip \(C\) with the canonical topology. Note that the covering families of \(C\) are the surjective families of maps and that the covering families are non-empty. Note moreover that there are, up to isomorphism, only two constant sheaves on \(C\): the sheaf with value the empty set and the sheaf with value the one-element set. Set \(C = C'\) and let \(u : C \to C'\) be a constant functor. The functor \(u\) transforms the covering families of \(C\) into covering families of \(C'\). The functor \(u\) is not continuous. Indeed, since the representable presheaves of \(C'\) are sheaves, for every object \(X\) of \(C'\), there exists a sheaf \(F\) on \(C'\) such that the cardinality of the set \(F(X)\) is \(\geq 2\), and consequently the presheaf \(u^* F\) is not a sheaf.

footnotes.html: (∗) "Covering" instead of "bicovering" would not necessarily suffice, cf. example 1.9.3 below.
(∗) In fact, it suffices that \(u\) commute with the fibre products occurring in the base changes for morphisms coming from covering families for \(T\).
(1) indexed by the sets belonging to a suitable universe.
(2) One can in fact show that this condition is always satisfied.

blocks.html: 2. Cocontinuous functors

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. We say that \(u\) is cocontinuous if it possesses the following property:

(COC) For every object \(Y\) of \(C\) and for every covering sieve \(R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\), the sieve of \(Y\) generated by the arrows \(Z \to Y\) such that \(u(Z) \to u(Y)\) factors through \(R\), covers \(Y\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2

Let \(C\) be a small site, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. We denote by \(\widehat{u}_* : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C}'\) the right adjoint functor of the functor \(F \mapsto F \circ u = \widehat{u}^* F\) (I 5.1). The functor \(u\) is cocontinuous if and only if for every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\), \(\widehat{u}_* G\) is a sheaf on \(C'\).

Proof. The condition is sufficient. Suppose that for every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\), the presheaf \(\widehat{u}_* G\) is a sheaf. Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C\) and \(R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\) a covering sieve. We have an isomorphism \(\mathrm{Hom}(u(Y), \widehat{u}_* G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(R, \widehat{u}_* G)\), whence by adjunction (I 5.1) an isomorphism \(\mathrm{Hom}(\widehat{u}^* \circ u(Y), G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(\widehat{u}^* R, G)\). We deduce (II 5.3) that the morphism \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) is bicovering. But the functor \(\widehat{u}^*\) commutes with projective limits and consequently the morphism \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) is a monomorphism. It is therefore a covering monomorphism. On the other hand we have a canonical morphism \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) deduced from the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id}_C \to \widehat{u}^* u\), (I 5.4 3)). Let us then make the base change \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\). We obtain a sieve covering \(Y\): \[ \widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* u(Y)} Y \longrightarrow Y , \] and when one seeks the arrows \(Z \to Y\) which factor through this sieve, one obtains the sieve described by property (COC).

The condition is necessary: Let \(S\) be an object of \(C'\) and \(R \hookrightarrow S\) a sieve covering \(S\). We must show that for every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\) we have an isomorphism \[ \mathrm{Hom}(S, \widehat{u}_* G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(R, \widehat{u}_* G) . \] Then, using proposition II 5.3 and the adjunction isomorphisms, one sees that it suffices to show that the monomorphism \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* S\) is covering. For this, it suffices to show (II 5.1) that for every base change \(Y \to \widehat{u}^* S\) the sieve \(\widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* S} Y\) is covering, (\(Y\) an object of \(C\)). But, by the properties of adjoint functors and I 5.4 3), the morphism \(Y \to \widehat{u}^* S\) factors through \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y) \to \widehat{u}^* S\), and consequently the sieve \(\widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* S} Y \to Y\) is the transform under the base change \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) of the monomorphism \(\widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* S} \widehat{u}^* u(Y) \xrightarrow{\ q\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\). Now the functor \(\widehat{u}^*\) commutes with projective limits, and consequently the monomorphism \(q\) is the transform under \(\widehat{u}^*\) of the sieve \(R \times_S u(Y) \hookrightarrow u(Y)\), which is covering. Hypothesis (COC) then allows us to say that the sieve \(\widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* S} Y \to Y\) is covering, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(u : C \to C'\) a cocontinuous functor. We denote by \(u^* : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) the functor \(u^* = a \widehat{u}^* i'\), where \(a\) denotes the "associated sheaf" functor for \(C\), \(\widehat{u}^*\) the functor \(F \mapsto F \circ u\), \(i'\) the inclusion functor \(\widetilde{C}' \to \widehat{C}'\).

  1. 1)

    The functor \(u^*\) commutes with inductive limits and is exact.

  2. 2)

    We have a canonical isomorphism \(u^* a' \simeq a \widehat{u}^*\), where \(a'\) denotes the "associated sheaf" functor for \(\widehat{C}'\).

  3. 3)

    The functor \(u^*\) admits a right adjoint \(u_* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\). When \(C\) is small, the diagram \[ (2.3.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]^-{u_*} \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_-{i} & \widetilde{C}' \ar@{^{(}->}[d]^-{i'} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[r]_-{\widehat{u}_*} & \widehat{C}' } \] where the bottom functor is right adjoint to the functor \(\widehat{u}^*\) (I 5.1), is commutative up to canonical isomorphism.

  4. 4)

    Let \(\mathcal{V} \supset \mathcal{U}\) be a universe. We denote by \(u_{*\mathcal{U}} : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \to \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(u_{*\mathcal{V}} : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \to \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{V}}\)) the right adjoint functor relative to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)) whose existence is affirmed in 3). The diagram \[ (2.3.2) \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[r]^-{u_{*\mathcal{U}}} \ar[d] & \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[d] \\ \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \ar[r]_-{u_{*\mathcal{V}}} & \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{V}} } \] is commutative up to isomorphism.

Proof. Assertions 1) and 2) follow immediately from II 3.4. Assertion 3), when \(C\) is small, follows from 2.2. When \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, it will be proved in 4.4. Assertion 4), when \(C\) is small, follows from the analogous commutativity assertion when the topologies on \(C\) and \(C'\) are chaotic and from I 3.5. When the topologies on \(C\) and \(C'\) are chaotic, the commutativity of (2.3.2) is seen immediately from the explicit description of \(u_*\) (I 5.1).

We shall not develop here the considerations relating to the \(\gamma\)-objects of the categories of sheaves. It will suffice for us to note that the functors \(u^*\) and \(u_*\) introduced in this section always commute with finite projective limits (contrary to what happened in the preceding section for the functor \(u^s\)). Consequently they extend naturally to functors defined on the \(\gamma\)-objects, which are adjoint to one another and which commute with the "underlying sheaf of sets" functors. We shall make the abuses of notation indicated in 1.8, consisting in denoting by \(u^*\) and \(u_*\) the extensions to the \(\gamma\)-objects.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(C \overset{v}{\underset{u}{\rightleftarrows}} C'\) a pair of functors, where \(v\) is left adjoint to \(u\). The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The functor \(u\) is continuous.

  2. ii)

    The functor \(v\) is cocontinuous.

Moreover, under these equivalent conditions, we have canonical isomorphisms \(v_* \simeq u_s\), \(v^* \simeq u^s\). In particular, the functor \(u^s\) commutes with finite projective limits.

Proof. The property for a functor of being continuous or cocontinuous does not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) for which \(C\) and \(C'\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites (this is immediate in the case of a cocontinuous functor, and it follows from 1.5 in the case of a continuous functor). We may therefore, at the cost of enlarging the universe, suppose that \(C\) and \(C'\) are small. The proposition then follows from 2.2 and I 5.6.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6

Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a continuous and cocontinuous functor between two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites. Then the functor \(u^* : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) (2.3) commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive and projective limits. We denote by \(u_! : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\) and \(u_* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\) the left and right adjoint functors of \(u^*\) respectively. The functor \(u_!\) is fully faithful if and only if the functor \(u_*\) is fully faithful. When \(u\) is fully faithful, \(u_!\) is fully faithful, and the converse is true when the topologies of \(C\) and \(C'\) are coarser than the canonical topology.

The functor \(u^*\) admits a right adjoint \(u_*\) (2.3) and a left adjoint \(u_!\) (1.2). The functor \(u^*\) therefore commutes with inductive limits and projective limits (I 2.11). The fact that the functor \(u_!\) is fully faithful if and only if the functor \(u_*\) is fully faithful is a general property of adjoint functors (I 5.7.1). When \(u\) is fully faithful, the functor \(\widehat{u}_* : \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \to \widehat{C}'_{\mathcal{V}}\) relative to \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves, for a sufficiently large universe \(\mathcal{V}\), is fully faithful (I 5.7). Consequently the functor \(u_* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\) is fully faithful by virtue of the commutativity of (2.3.1) and (2.3.2), hence \(u_!\) is fully faithful by what precedes. The converse follows from the existence of the commutative diagram 1.2 iv), taking into account the fact that the functors \(\varepsilon_C\) and \(\varepsilon_{C'}\) are fully faithful when the topologies are coarser than the canonical topology, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 2.7

With the notation of 1.9.2, the functor \[ \varphi : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ouv}(X) \] is continuous (1.9.2) and cocontinuous (2.2). Moreover, let \(i : Y \to X\) be the canonical injection and \(i^{-1} : \mathrm{Ouv}(X) \to \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)\) the functor it enables one to define (1.9.1). The functor \(i^{-1}\) is right adjoint to the functor \(\varphi\). We thus have a sequence of three adjoint functors: \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \varphi^s & , & \varphi_s \\ & & \| \\ & & \varphi^* \ , \ \varphi_* \end{array} \] and canonical isomorphisms \(\varphi^* \simeq (i^{-1})^s\), \(\varphi_* \simeq i^{-1}_s\).
3. Induced topology

Let \(C'\) be a site, \(C\) a category and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor. For every universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(C'\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(C\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category, we denote by \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) the finest among the topologies \(T\) on \(C\) which make \(u\) continuous (1.1). (Such a topology exists thanks to II 2.2). The topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) does not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\). Indeed, if \(\mathcal{V} \supset \mathcal{U}\) is a universe we have \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}} = \mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) (1.1 and 1.5). The topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is called the topology induced on \(C\) by the topology of \(C'\) by means of the functor \(u\)(1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2

Let \(C\) be a small category, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(u : C \to C'\) a functor, \(\mathscr{C}\) the topology on \(C\) induced by \(u\). Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and \(R \hookrightarrow X\) a sieve of \(X\). The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) is covering for \(\mathscr{C}\).

  2. ii)

    For every base change \(Y \to X\), where \(Y\) is an object of \(C\), the morphism \(u_!(R \times_X Y) \to u(Y)\) is bicovering in \(\widehat{C}'\) (II 5.2).

Proof. i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii) follows from axiom (T1) of topologies and from 1.2. ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i): For every sheaf \(F\) on \(C'\), the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(Y, u^* F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(R \times_X Y, u^* F) \] is isomorphic, by adjunction (I 5.1), to the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(u(Y), F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(u_!(R \times_X Y), F) \] which is bijective (II 5.3). Consequently (II 2.2) the sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) is covering for \(\mathscr{C}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3

Let \(C'\) be a site, \(C\) a category, \(u : C \to C'\) a functor, \(\mathscr{C}\) the topology on \(C\) induced by the topology of \(C'\). Let \((X_i \to X)\) \(i \in I\) be a family of squarable morphisms of \(C\) and suppose that \(u\) commutes with fibre products.(∗) The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The family \(X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), is covering for \(\mathscr{C}\).

  2. ii)

    The family \((u(X_i) \to u(X))\), \(i \in I\), is covering.

Proof. i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii) follows from 1.6. ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i): Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe such that \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small and \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. Let \(R \hookrightarrow X\) be the sieve generated by the \(X_i \to X\). The presheaf \(R\) is the cokernel of the pair of arrows (I 2.12 and I 3.5) \[ \coprod_{i,j} X_i \times_X X_j \rightrightarrows \coprod_i X_i \] (the direct sum is taken here in \(\widehat{C}\)). Since the functor \(u_!\) commutes with inductive limits (I 5.4), the presheaf \(u_! R\) is the cokernel of the pair of arrows \[ \coprod_{i,j} u(X_i \times_X X_j) \rightrightarrows \coprod_i u(X_i) . \] Since the functor \(u\) commutes with fibre products, the presheaf \(u_! R\) is the cokernel of the pair of arrows \[ \coprod_{i,j} u(X_i) \times_{u(X)} u(X_j) \rightrightarrows \coprod_i u(X_i) , \] and consequently \(u_! R \to u(X)\) is a sieve of \(u(X)\) generated by the \(u(X_i) \to u(X)\), \(i \in I\). Using once again the fact that \(u\) commutes with fibre products, one shows that for every base change \(Y \to X\), where \(Y\) is an object of \(C\), \(u_!(R \times_X Y) \to u(Y)\) is a sieve of \(u(Y)\) generated by the \(u(X_i) \times_{u(X)} u(Y) \to u(Y)\), \(i \in I\). Since the family \(u(X_i) \to u(X)\), \(i \in I\), is covering, the family \(u(X_i) \times_{u(X)} u(Y) \to u(Y)\), \(i \in I\), is covering. Hence \(u_!(R \times_X Y) \to u(Y)\) is a covering sieve and consequently (3.2) \(R \hookrightarrow X\) is covering for \(\mathscr{C}\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4

Let \(C'\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(C\) a full subcategory of \(C'\), \(u : C \to C'\) the inclusion functor. Suppose that the fibre products are representable in \(C\) and that \(u\) commutes with fibre products. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. i)

    a) For every object \(X\) of \(C\), every covering family \((Y_j \to X)\), \(j \in J\), of \(C'\) is refined by a covering family \(X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), where the \(X_i\) are objects of \(C\).

    b) There exists a small set \(G\) of objects of \(C\), such that every object of \(C\) is the target of a covering family in \(C'\) of morphisms whose sources are in \(G\).

  2. ii)

    The topology induced by the topology of \(C'\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology (II 3.0.2) and the functor \(u\) is continuous and cocontinuous for this topology.
Proof. Follows immediately from 3.3 and 2.1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.5

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) the canonical functor (II 4.4.0). Let us equip \(\widetilde{C}\) with the canonical topology. Then the topology of the site \(C\) is the topology induced by the topology of \(\widetilde{C}\).

Proof. The covering families of \(\widetilde{C}\) for the canonical topology are the universal effective epimorphic families (II 2.5), i.e. (II 4.3) the epimorphic families. Let \(T\) be the topology of the site \(C\) and \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) the finest of the topologies \(T'\) on \(C\) such that for every sheaf \(F\) on \(\widetilde{C}\), \(F \circ \varepsilon_C\) is a sheaf for \(T'\). It suffices to show that \(T = \mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\), for then \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology and consequently \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is the induced topology.

A) The topology \(T\) is finer than \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\): Let \((X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), be a family covering for \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\). Then for every sheaf \(F\) on \(\widetilde{C}\), \(F(\varepsilon_C(X)) \to \prod_i F(\varepsilon_C(X_i))\) is injective and consequently (II 5.2) \((\varepsilon_C X_i \to \varepsilon_C X)\), \(i \in I\), is covering for the canonical topology of \(\widetilde{C}\), hence (II 5.2) \((X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), is covering for \(T\).

B) The topology \(T\) is coarser than \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\): It suffices to show that \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) is continuous (1.1). Now we shall show in IV no. 1 that every sheaf on \(\widetilde{C}\) is representable and consequently, for every sheaf \(F\) on \(\widetilde{C}\), \(F \circ \varepsilon_C\) is a sheaf on \(C\). (We shall not use 3.5 until IV 1).
We note two results which will be used in VI 7.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6

Let \((C_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of sites, \(C\) a category and for every \(i \in I\), \(u_i : C_i \to C\) a functor, \(\mathcal{U}\) a universe such that the categories \(C_i\) and \(C\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. There exists a topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) on \(C\) which is the coarsest of the topologies for which the \(u_i\) are continuous. The topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) does not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) for which the categories under consideration are small.
The last assertion of 3.6 follows from 1.5.

Let \(T\) be a topology on \(C\). Then the functors \(u_i\) are continuous if and only if for every \(i \in I\) and for every covering sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) of an object \(X\) of \(C_i\), the morphism \[ u_{i!}(R) \longrightarrow u_i(X) \] of \(\widehat{C}\) is bicovering (1.2 (ii)). Hence 3.6 is a consequence of the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.6.1

Let \(C\) be a small category, \((u_i : F_i \to G_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of arrows of \(\widehat{C}\). Then there exists on \(C\) a coarsest topology among those which make the morphisms \(u_i\) covering (resp. bicovering) (II 5.2).

To say that \(u : F \to G\) is covering for a given topology \(T\) means that for every arrow \(X \to G\), with \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), the corresponding arrow \(F \times_G X \to X\) is covering, or, equivalently, that the family of arrows \(X' \to X\) of \(C\) which factor through the preceding arrow is covering. The fact that there exists a coarsest topology among those for which the \(u_i : F_i \to G_i\) are covering thus follows from I 1.1.6, whence the non-resp. assertion of 3.6.1. The resp. assertion is deduced from it, upon recalling that a morphism \(u : F \to G\) is bicovering if and only if the morphisms \(u : F \to G\) and \(\mathrm{diag}_u : F \to F \times_G F\) are covering.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.7

Let \((C_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of sites, \(C\) a category, for each \(i \in I\), \(u_i : C_i \to C\) a functor, and \(\mathcal{U}\) a universe such that the categories \(C_i\) and \(C\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. There exists a topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) which is the finest for which the \(u_i\) are cocontinuous. The topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) does not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) for which the categories under consideration are small.

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe for which the categories under consideration are small. The functors \(u_i\) are cocontinuous for a topology \(\mathscr{C}\) on \(C\) if and only if for every \(i \in I\) and every sheaf \(F\) on \(C_i\) the presheaf \(\widehat{u}_{i*} F\) is a sheaf for \(\mathscr{C}\) (2.2). It follows that the topology \(\mathscr{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is the finest topology for which the presheaves \(\widehat{u}_{i*} F\), \(i \in I\), \(F \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_i\), are sheaves (II 2.2). The last assertion follows from 2.2.

footnotes.html: (1) When no confusion results, this topology is called the topology induced on \(C\) by the topology of \(C'\).
(∗) In fact, it suffices that \(u\) commute with fibre products of the form \(X_i \times_X X'\).

blocks.html: 4. Comparison lemma

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1 (comparison lemma)

Let \(C\) be a small category, \(C'\) a site whose underlying category is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and \(u : C \to C'\) a fully faithful functor. Endow \(C\) with the topology induced by \(u\) (3.1). Consider the properties:

  1. i)

    Every object of \(C'\) can be covered by objects coming from \(C\).

  2. ii)

    The functor \(F \mapsto F \circ u\) induces an equivalence of categories from the category of sheaves on \(C'\) to the category of sheaves on \(C\).

One always has i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). When \(C'\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and when the topology of \(C'\) is coarser than the canonical topology, one has ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i).
Let us first prove i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). The proof is carried out in two steps.

First step. For every presheaf \(H\) of \(\widehat{C}'\) the adjunction morphism \(\varphi : u_! u^* H \to H\) (I 5.1) is bicovering (II 5.3) and the functor \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) (1.1.1) is fully faithful.

Let \(C/H\) be the small category whose objects are the objects \(Y\) of \(C\) equipped with a morphism \(u(Y) \to H\), and whose morphisms are the commutative diagrams: \[ \xymatrix{ u(Y) \ar[rr]^-{u(m)} \ar[dr] & & u(Y') \ar[dl] \\ & H & } \] One has \(u^* H = \varinjlim_{Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, C/H} Y\) (I 3.4) and consequently (I 5.4) \(u_! u^* H = \varinjlim_{Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, C/H} u(Y)\). The adjunction morphism is the obvious morphism which results from the description of \(u_! u^* H\) as an inductive limit. The morphism \(\varphi\) has the following property: (∗) For every object \(Y\) of \(C\), every morphism \(m : u(Y) \to H\) factors uniquely as the canonical morphism \(\alpha(m) : u(Y) \to u_! u^* H\) followed by the morphism \(\varphi\). It follows immediately from i) that the morphism \(\varphi\) is covering (II 5.1); let us show that it is bicovering. Let \(p, q : Z \rightrightarrows u_! u^* H\) be two morphisms from an object \(Z\) of \(\widehat{C}'\), such that \(\varphi p = \varphi q\). For every object \(Y\) of \(C\) and every morphism \(n : u(Y) \to Z\), one has \(\varphi p n = \varphi q n\). Property (∗) then implies that \(p n = q n\), and since the \(u(Y)\) cover \(Z\), the kernel of \((p, q)\) is a sieve covering \(Z\). The morphism \(\varphi\) is therefore bicovering (II 5.3). For every sheaf \(H\) on \(C'\), \(u^* H\) is a sheaf on \(C\) denoted \(u_s H\) (1.1.1). One has moreover \(u^s u_s H = a' u_! u_s H\) (1.3), and the adjunction morphism \(u^s u_s H \to H\) is obtained by applying the functor "associated sheaf" to the morphism \(\varphi : u_! u^* H \to H\). Consequently (II 5.3) the adjunction morphism \(u^s u_s H \to H\) is an isomorphism. Therefore \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) is fully faithful.

Second step. The functor \(u\) is cocontinuous and the functor \(u^s : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\) (1.2) is fully faithful. Consequently \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) is an equivalence. Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C\) and \(i : R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\) a covering sieve. Since the functor \(u^*\) commutes with projective limits (I 5.5) the morphism \(u^*(i) : u^*(R) \hookrightarrow u^* u(Y)\) is a monomorphism. Since \(u\) is fully faithful, one has \(u^* u(Y) \simeq Y\), whence a sieve of \(Y\), \(u^*(i) : u^*(R) \to Y\). To show that \(u\) is cocontinuous, it suffices to show that \(u^*(i) : u^*(R) \to Y\) is a covering sieve for the topology induced on \(C\) (2.1). For this, it suffices to show (3.2) that for every base change \(m : X \to Y\), the morphism \(u_!(u^*(R) \times_Y X) \to u(X)\) is bicovering. But since \(u^*\) commutes with projective limits, one has \(u^*(R) \times_Y X = u^*(R \times_{u(Y)} u(X))\) and \(R \times_{u(Y)} u(X)\) is a sieve covering \(u(X)\). It therefore suffices to show that for every object \(Y\) of \(C\) and every covering sieve \(i : R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\), the morphism of \(\widehat{C}'\), \(u_! u^*(R) \xrightarrow{\ u_! u^*(i)\ } u(Y)\), is bicovering. Now this morphism factors as the adjunction morphism \(u_! u^*(R) \to R\), which is bicovering (first step), and the monomorphism \(R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\) which is covering. It is therefore bicovering (II 5.3). This shows that \(u\) is cocontinuous. Since \(u\) is continuous and fully faithful, it follows from 2.6 (used in the case where \(C\) is small) that \(u^s\) (denoted \(u_!\) in 2.6) is fully faithful. Since \(u^s\) and \(u_s\) are adjoint to one another and are fully faithful, they are quasi-inverse functors and consequently \(u_s\) is an equivalence.

Let us now prove that ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). The objects \(Y\) of \(C\) form a generating family of \(\widetilde{C}\) (II 4.10) and consequently, for every object \(X\) of \(C'\), there exists an epimorphic family (in \(\widetilde{C}\)) \(v_i : Y_i \to u_s X\), \(i \in I\). One has \(u_s u(Y_i) = Y_i\) and, the functor \(u_s\) being an equivalence of categories, one has \(v_i = u_s(w_i)\), where the \(w_i : u(Y_i) \to X\) form an epimorphic family of \(\widetilde{C}'\). It then follows from II 5.1 that the family \(w_i : u(Y_i) \to X\), \(i \in I\), is covering.
4.2. End of the proof of 1.2.

Let \(G\) be a full subcategory of \(C\) whose objects form a small topologically generating family of \(C\) (II 3.0.1). Endow \(G\) with the topology induced by the inclusion functor \(i : G \to C\) (3.1). The functor \((u \circ i)_s = i_s \circ u_s\) (1.1.1) admits a left adjoint according to the first part of the proof of 1.2. Since \(i_s\) is an equivalence of categories (4.1), the functor \(u_s\) admits a left adjoint \(u^s\) and one has a functorial isomorphism \(u^s \simeq (u \circ i)^s \circ i_s\). Let us show that the diagram \[ (4.2.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_C} & C' \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_{C'}} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' } \] is commutative up to isomorphism. For every sheaf \(H\) on \(C'\), one has \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}'}(\varepsilon_{C'} u X, H) \simeq u_s H(X)\), for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\). One has moreover \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}'}(u^s \varepsilon_C X, H) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}}(\varepsilon_C X, u_s H)\) by adjunction, then \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}}(\varepsilon_C X, u_s H) \simeq u_s H(X)\) by definition of \(\varepsilon_C\). Whence an isomorphism \(\varepsilon_{C'} u X \simeq u^s \varepsilon_C X\) for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\). This proves i) \(\Longrightarrow\) iv). Let us show that iv) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). One has a commutative diagram \[ (4.2.2) \qquad \xymatrix{ G \ar[r]^-{i} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_G} & C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_C} & C' \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_{C'}} \\ \widetilde{G} \ar[r]_-{i^s} & \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' , } \] and consequently, according to the first part of the proof, the functor \(i \circ u : G \to C'\) is continuous. One deduces immediately by 4.1 and 1.1 that \(u\) is continuous, whence iv) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). One obtains moreover the uniqueness of \(u^s\); knowing, from the first part of the proof, the uniqueness when \(C\) is small.
4.3. End of the proof of 1.5 and 1.7.

Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a functor between two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(G\) a full subcategory of \(C\) whose set of objects is a small topologically generating family of \(C\) (II 3.0.1). Endow \(G\) with the topology induced by the inclusion functor \(i : G \to C\). It follows immediately from 4.1 and 1.1 that \(u\) is continuous if and only if \(u \circ i\) is continuous. From this remark and the first part of the proof of 1.5 the general case follows. This remark also allows one to reduce the proof of 1.7 to the case where the category \(C\) is small.
4.4. End of the proof of 2.3.

Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a functor between two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites, \(G\) a full subcategory of \(C\) whose set of objects is a small topologically generating family of \(C\) (II 3.0.1), endowed with the topology induced by the inclusion functor \(i : G \to C\). It follows from the proof of 4.1 (4.1.1 second step) that \(i\) is cocontinuous. Consequently, when \(u\) is cocontinuous, the functor \(u \circ i : G \to C'\) is cocontinuous. Moreover, \(i^* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{G}\) is an equivalence of categories (4.1). Therefore the functor \(u^* : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) admits a right adjoint. This proves 3). To prove 4), it suffices to remark that \((u \circ i)_* \simeq u_* \circ i_*\) and that \(i_*\) is an equivalence (4.1). The commutativity of (2.3.2) then follows from the commutativity of these diagrams when \(C\) is small.
5. Localization

Now let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(X\) an object of \(\widehat{C}\). Unless expressly stated otherwise, the category \(C/X\) will be endowed with the topology \(\mathscr{C}\) induced by the functor \(j_X : C/X \to C\) (3.1). The notation \(C/X\) will denote the category \(C/X\) endowed with the topology \(\mathscr{C}\). Proposition I 5.11 shows us that the functor \(j_{X!}\) commutes with fibre products and consequently transforms every monomorphism into a monomorphism. In particular, for every object \((Y \to X)\) of \(C/X\), the functor \(j_{X!}\) establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the sieves, in the category \(C/X\), of the object \((Y \to X)\) and the sieves, in \(C\), of the object \(Y\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(X\) an object of \(\widehat{C}\) and \(j_X : C/X \to C\) the corresponding continuous functor.

  1. 1)

    A sieve \(R\) of an object \((Z \to X)\) is covering in \(C/X\) if and only if the sieve \(j_{X!}(R) \hookrightarrow Z\) is covering in \(C\).

  2. 2)

    The functor \(j_X : C/X \to C\) is cocontinuous and continuous.

  3. 3)

    Let \(m : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). One then has the commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ C/Y \ar[rr]^-{j_m} \ar[dr]_-{j_Y} & & C/X \ar[dl]^-{j_X} \\ & C & } \] The topology induced by the functor \(j_Y\) on \(C/Y\) is equal to the topology induced by \(j_m\) on \(C/Y\).

  4. 4)

    The topology induced by \(j_X : C/X \to C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology (II 3.0.2).
Proof. 1) If the sieve \(R\) of \((Z \to X)\) is covering, the sieve \(j_{X!}(R) \hookrightarrow Z\) is covering (1.6).

Conversely, if the sieve \(j_{X!}(R) \to Z\) is covering in \(C\), one sees that the same holds for every sieve obtained by making a base change in \(C/X\). The sieve \(R\) is therefore covering (3.2).
2) Follows immediately from 1) by applying 2.1.
3) Follows immediately from the description of covering sieves given by 1).

4) Let \((G)_i\), \(i \in I\), be a small topologically generating family of \(C\). One verifies immediately that the small family \((u : G_i \to X)\), \(u \in \coprod_{i \in I} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(G_i, X)\), is topologically generating in \(C/X\).
Terminology and notation 5.3.

According to the preceding proposition the functor \(j_X\) is both a continuous and a cocontinuous functor. It therefore defines a sequence of three adjoint functors (4.3.2) between the categories of sheaves of sets (1.3 and 2.3): \[ \begin{aligned} j_X^s \ &: \ (C/X)^{\sim} \to \widetilde{C} \\ j_X^* = j_{X,s} \ &: \ \widetilde{C} \to (C/X)^{\sim} \\ j_{X*} \ &: \ (C/X)^{\sim} \to \widetilde{C} . \end{aligned} \] In the particular situation of proposition 5.2 we shall use the following terminology and notation:

1. 1)

    The functor \(j_{X*}\) will be called the direct image functor.

  2. 2)

    The functor \(j_{X,s} = j_X^*\) will be denoted \(j_X^*\) and will be called the functor of restriction to \(C/X\).

  3. 3)

    The functor \(j_X^s\) on sheaves of sets will be called the "functor of extension by the empty set to the category \(C\)" and will be denoted \(j_{X!}\) (cf. 1.9.2).
One thus has a sequence of three adjoint functors between \((C/X)^{\sim}\) and \(\widetilde{C}\): \[ j_{X!} \ , \ j_X^* \ , \ j_{X*} . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.4

The functor \(j_{X!} : (C/X)^{\sim} \to \widetilde{C}\) factors through the category \(\widetilde{C}/aX\) (\(a\) is the associated sheaf functor): \[ (C/X)^{\sim} \xrightarrow{\ e_X^{\sim}\ } \widetilde{C}/aX \to \widetilde{C} . \] The functor: \[ e_X^{\sim} \ : \ (C/X)^{\sim} \longrightarrow \widetilde{C}/aX \] is an equivalence of categories. The functor of restriction to \(C/X\), composed with the equivalence \(e_X^{\sim}\), is isomorphic to the functor "base change by \(aX \to e\)" (\(e\) the final object of \(\widetilde{C}\)): \(F \mapsto (F \times aX \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{pr}_2\ } aX)\).

Proof. The image under \(j_{X!}\) of the final object of \((C/X)^{\sim}\) is the object \(aX\); whence the factorization. To show that the functor \(e_X^{\sim}\) is an equivalence, we shall limit ourselves to a few indications. By I 5.11, a presheaf on \(C/X\) is defined by a presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) equipped with a morphism \(F \to X\). One then proves that the following two properties are equivalent:

1. i)

    The presheaf on \(C/X\) defined by \(F \to X\) is a sheaf.

  2. ii)

    The following diagram is cartesian (one denotes by \(i\) and \(a\) the functors injection into presheaves, and associated sheaf): \[ \xymatrix{ F \ar[r] \ar[d] & i a F \ar[d] \\ X \ar[r] & i a X , } \]
One then immediately deduces that \(e_X^{\sim}\) is an equivalence. The last assertion is trivial.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5

1) Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(X\) an object of \(\widehat{C}\). The diagram below of categories and functors is commutative up to canonical isomorphisms: \[ \xymatrix@C=2.6em{ C/X \ar[r]^-{h_X} \ar@{=}[d] & (C/X)^{\wedge} \ar[r]^-{a_X} \ar[d]^-{e_X^{\wedge}} & (C/X)^{\sim} \ar[r]^-{i_X} \ar[d]^-{e_X^{\sim}} & (C/X)^{\wedge} \ar[d]^-{e^{\wedge}/X} & \\ C/X \ar[r]_-{h/X} & \widehat{C}/X \ar[r]_-{a/X} & \widetilde{C}/aX \ar[r]_-{i/aX} & \widehat{C}/iaX \ar[r]_-{\pi} & \widehat{C}/X . } \] The notations \(a_X\) and \(i_X\) denote the functors "associated sheaf" and injection into presheaves for the site \(C/X\). The notation \(a/X\) denotes the natural extension of the functor \(a\) (associated sheaf for the site \(C\)) to the category of arrows with target \(X\), and similarly for the notation \(i/aX\). Finally the notation \(\pi\) denotes the base change functor by the canonical arrow \(X \to iaX\).

2) Let moreover \(m : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). The diagram below is commutative up to canonical isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \widetilde{C}/aX/aY \ar@{=}[dd] & & (C/X)^{\sim}/a_X Y \ar[ll]_-{f} \ar[dr]^-{g} & \\ & & & (C/X/Y)^{\sim} \ar[dl]^-{e_m^{\sim}} \\ \widetilde{C}/aY & & (C/Y)^{\sim} \ar[ll]^-{e_Y^{\sim}} & } \]

The arrow \(f\) is the natural extension of the equivalence \(e^{\sim}/X\) to the category of arrows with target \(a_X Y\), and is consequently an equivalence of categories. The arrow \(g\) is none other than the equivalence of 5.4 applied to the situation \((C/X)/[m]\).

3) Denote by \(j_{aX!} : \widetilde{C}/aX \to \widetilde{C}\) the functor "forget \(aX\)", and by \(j_{aX}^* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}/aX\) the functor "product by \(aX\)". The diagrams below are commutative up to canonical isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ (C/X)^{\sim} \ar[r]^-{j_{X!}} \ar[d] & \widetilde{C} \ar@{=}[d] \\ \widetilde{C}/aX \ar[r]_-{j_{aX!}} & \widetilde{C} } \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]^-{j_X^*} \ar@{=}[d] & (C/X)^{\sim} \ar[d]^-{e^{\sim}/X} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{j_{aX}^*} & \widetilde{C}/aX } \]
Proof. The proof of these assertions is immediate from the definition of the equivalences \(e_X^{\sim}\) (5.4) and \(e_X^{\wedge}\) (I 5.11).
